title: Breaking and Entering: Now or Never with Elise Peyronnet
transcript:
A conversation with Elise Peyronnet about Now or Never, broadcast on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, 2 July 2026.

joined by the Artistic Director of the festival, Elise Peyronnet, is with me in the studio.

Hey, Elise.

Hi, Lauren.

Lovely to catch up with you again.

You and I go way back to your Melbourne Music Week days many, many moons ago.

That's true, actually.

Yeah, we've known each other for a little while.

But thank you so much for having me today.

Yeah, thank you for joining me.

And, yeah, an incredible line-up that you've put together for what is now, yeah, I guess the fourth year of the festival,

which was originally sort of born as a combination of Melbourne Music Week and Melbourne Knowledge Week,

combining forces and now is City of Melbourne's sort of annual festival, spanning art, ideas, sound and technology.

I guess we'll get into some of the specifics of some of the events in a moment.

But I guess to start, this year's curatorial theme for Now or Never is A Whole New World.

Can you tell me about, I guess, your vision as the Artistic Director and how that theme, A Whole New World, shapes this year's program?

Well, the theme was chosen many, many months ago.

And I guess, as, you know, the world unfolded and just looking at, you know, everything that's happening geopolitically,

we are absolutely in a whole new world.

But initially, the theme was really talking to, I guess, the technological shifts that we are seeing in our everyday life.

Of course, we talk a lot about, you know, AI and just, we are only just starting to see the impact of it.

So I think we wanted to have a theme that was broad enough to really discuss that, the fact,

and maybe not necessarily fearing it, but making the, just the, just mentioning that we are indeed in a whole new world.

And I think for a curatorial theme, in terms of talks, it's interesting to, to, to cover that.

But also in terms of even creating events, there are a lot of the events around the city where we are going to take over buildings and changing maybe the experience that people will have from the different areas in the city.

And that is also inviting the audience to step into a whole new world.

Incredible.

I might just get you to switch mics for me.

Sorry, Elise.

I'm having some issues with that one.

Yeah, I was going to, you mentioned AI and I guess, yeah, being a festival that covers like technology as one of its sort of core pillars.

So I imagine, yeah, your curatorial team and programming team are having some big conversations around that as well with, you know, the ways in which we understand knowledge, feel like they're being sort of reshaped at the moment.

How have you been sort of navigating that, that current shift in other ways that it's, yeah, reflected within the program?

I mean, it's, yes, it's a, it's a current theme and one that we, I think, grasping, still grasping with.

This, it's a, you know, a really hot topic for artists as well.

I know that we have also discussed this topic since the beginning of Now or Never.

In fact, Now or Never was created in 2023.

So already in 2022, it was really the beginning also of AI in the everyday life.

So, yeah, it's always been a core topic, but I think it is, we question it, but it's also, it is here, we, probably all of us use it every day, you know, everyday life.

But it is indeed scary when it's brought to the light of, you know, of, in an artistic sense, you know, does it replace, you know, does it replace, you know, does it replace really the human agency and the artistic expression or not?

And it's just a tool that can enhance.

We're still at the beginning of that conversation.

Totally.

And there's a few, yeah, I guess, events happening as part of the program that sort of do, yeah, reflect on that for sure.

The festival itself runs across, yeah, 12 days.

Now or Never is a huge program, more than 250 local and international artists and creatives.

You've got over 150 events.

Where do you start putting a program like this together?

Was there a particular moment for you that sort of locked in first with the program?

It always comes from the venues, the locations.

And we have now worked for, since the beginning, with creating really unique experiences at the Royal Exhibition Building.

So I think that's one of the concepts that we started to work on, but that took a really long time to come to fruition.

So again, like spaces and looking at the city and where we want to place things, I think it's always, for me, starts there.

I guess, yeah, the City of Melbourne, the Now or Never Festival has a reputation for commissioning this really unique site-specific work.

I imagine, yeah, there's some creative challenges maybe with programming, sort of this cutting-edge technology events inside these buildings that are like centuries-year-old,

like the Royal Exhibition Building in Melbourne Town Hall.

Yeah, what sort of creative challenges have you faced?

But in fact, I mean, every year is a different one, but again, this year, it's a completely different take on the Royal Exhibition Building.

And we are bringing back a series, music, and a series of really slow-paced, meditative shows that are really kind of taking the counterpart of technology, in a way.

If anything, it is about slowing down and being in the moment.

And I think that that was an interesting balance to have in the program as well.

So if anything, in a way, we are going without technology, or it's not without technology, but really thinking about being in the present and really experiencing music in a different way.

I guess, speaking of slowing down, there's an event that's slowing down so much, it's a mass sleepover slumber party, where you have the opportunity to sleep over at the Royal Exhibition Building with an event called Somnia, which sounds pretty incredible.

Can you talk us through that particular event?

Yes, so this is indeed quite a unique experience, where we invite the audience to come and take a bed.

The Royal Exhibition Building, we will have a durational concert show with multiple artists.

We have first [name uncertain: Mendigisca], who is an amazing saxophonist, but experimental artist who has worked with [name uncertain: Gaterina Barbieri], has really reinvented saxophone as an instrument.

And it's quite a physical experience.

You can hear him breathe through the instrument.

This is the first part of the night.

And after that, we have invited William Basinski, amazing American experimental composer, to come and perform continuously the series of four albums that he created, the Disintegration Loops, that are really a landmark, ambient work for a lot of music lovers.

So we were really looking for a piece of music that could have that pace, where we are inviting reflection and meditation.

The music is quite melancholic.

It is about, it's actually about disappearing.

It's about like digitalizing the tapes, actually, that he, the music that he had created.

And as he's playing them, the loops are disappearing and the music is disappearing.

So it's a very profound piece of music as well.

So it will go for six hours.

So you can decide to stay up, move around the venue or take the bed and just stay there.

And when you say take the bed, people don't have to bring their own bed.

Sorry.

Take the bed that you would have been assigned to.

And then we'll have a wake up moment and a little breakfast final moment before people exit the venue.

That sounds incredible.

Yeah, I actually listened to the whole of the, or the, one of the tracks of William Basinski's

The Disintegration Loops last night in preparation for this, this interview.

And yeah, it's sort of believed to have influenced many artists, like including Burial as an example

as well.

I guess what, what sort of things are you needing to consider to support the audience through

such like an intense sonic experience over those, those 10 hours?

I think we just want to give some, you know, comfort for the audience to really, I think it's important.

I think you experience music in a completely different way when you are lying down.

I think it's also linking maybe to the experience of the deep listening experiences that are really blossoming

everywhere.

Like there's, there's a lot more at the moment because maybe people are looking for a different

way of, of, of taking the music.

And I think that's what we are trying to emulate.

We're trying to really create a, an environment that will be, that will be conducive to, to, to, to this.

Is this a work that you've, you know, experienced yourself, um, before bringing this to Melbourne or?

No, no, it's a, we, I've always, uh, I've always wanted to do a sleep, uh, a sleep event.

Um, of course, we looked at, uh, Max Richter, uh, who performed, um, before in Australia.

And, um, but this, this was curated, especially for, for Melbourne, uh, with Melbourne in mind.

And, um, yes, the first of maybe many, we'll see how we go this year.

I'm sure you'd be advising people coming along to rug up as well, given it's the middle of

winter in Melbourne in the Royal Exhibition building.

Yes, yes, it's BYO for the bedding.

And for fans of, um, Philip Glass, there's a homage to the world-renowned American composer

as well as part of the festival.

Can you tell us about that event?

Yeah, again, it is, uh, this, uh, has been curated as part of a full series around, again,

that, uh, that meditative state.

And I mean, Philip Glass's music is, you know, that beautiful, repetitive,

minimalist music, um, he has influenced so many different composers into so many different

genres.

And I think when we program music, we're always look, always looking for, um, bringing some

diversity as well, and not just having electronic music, uh, based music where an art and technology

festival, but we're also looking at innovation and experimentation, uh, as being really the key,

um, driving factors for, for us programming some of those acts.

And, uh, Philip Glass, I mean, very amazing, amazing composer, as I was saying.

And, um, I really wanted to show, I wanted to bring that music that is usually presented in

concert halls in a, in a different environment, being the Royal Exhibition building.

We have the stage in the center with the, under the dome with, uh, the audience around it, um,

seated.

And I wanted to be accessible to as many people as possible who may, who may, who may, who

may, you know, want to discover that, uh, that music.

We have first, um, Orchestra Victoria.

We have like close to 30 musicians on stage, uh, performing a unique piece of Philip Glass

that is rarely performed alone.

Um, it's, it's a ballet piece initially.

And then we have [name uncertain: Maki Namikawa], who is this fantastic pianist, uh, soloist who, um, has worked

with, uh, Philip Glass, collaborated with him.

And she's going to perform the piano etude, uh, one to 10, which are really, really, again,

landmark, uh, piano works, but piano again, is very accessible.

Um, and, um, it's going to be a really beautiful night.

Thank you.

Gorgeous.

If you've just joined us on RRR, I have Elise Peyronnet from Now or Never, the artistic director

of the festival with me in the studio on RRR, running through the program that has just

been revealed.

And Elise, there's also a headline sort of late night music program at Melbourne

Town Hall that features, yeah, a whole bunch of artists across three nights, both local

and international.

Can you take us through, uh, some of the things happening at Melbourne Town Hall?

Yes.

So, well, Town Hall is going to be transformed for the full duration of the festival into going

to take different shapes.

Um, like we have Robin Fox first, who's going to, has a new, um, a new commission piece, a new

piece, uh, um, who's going to take over main hall.

It's an installation, like lots of lasers.

It's all around the room.

That is during the week free for the public to come.

We have invited, uh, to also present a new, new work, a new dance work inside, uh, town hall

as well.

So that's to start the festival.

And then as we move into the weekend, the second weekend, we change over the venue again into

more of a music, uh, music, uh, venue.

So we have three nights, um, where two of them we've invited local promoters.

We really wanted to maybe in the, the spirit of Melbourne music week and how we have worked in the past with lots of, um, our amazing independent

promoters that we have here in Melbourne.

And we've invited [name uncertain: Chileo club], um, which are amazing, um, like promoting Latin X, Latin club,

underground music, um, and has been doing that for many years, uh, mainly at Miscellenia in Melbourne.

But we really wanted to, to profile them and work with them.

Uh, they are bringing, they've curated an amazing lineup.

We have Aisha, we have Dinamarca, some artists that have actually never played here in Melbourne before.

Um, so very excited about that.

And [name uncertain: Zalina], who is the, the, well, the, the head on show, I guess, of, uh, [name uncertain: Chileo club] will be also performing.

And on the Saturday we have Octave One, uh, amazingly legendary, um, Detroit, uh, producers that are playing live.

Um, it's a really great live show, very big and, and, and fun to watch.

And in fact, all the entire, um, night is mainly built around live, like, uh, you know, um, artists playing with, uh, hardware, uh, equipment.

So we have Sleep D, uh, as well, and a hybrid man who is going to, to come and perform, um, on that night and Jeanette as well.

And then to close on the Sunday, we are bringing back My Disco, uh, who I think, uh, have not been performing for many years.

So it's kind of their, their return, uh, with us.

We're very excited about having them back.

What did you say to My Disco to get them to reform for you?

We, I think they, it was just apparently just the right time.

Um, I think, uh, they were, they were ready.

They, they wanted, they wanted to.

It didn't really take that much, I don't know.

Convincing.

Convincing, maybe.

And maybe what, what helped as well was that we knew that we had Robin Fox, uh, closing as well.

And they have been, you know, they're, they're close in their relationships and, and artistic endeavors.

So, uh, I think maybe that's what I would say that it's Robin who, um, influenced their decision.

And there's also, uh, Derrick Gee's Radio Hour, who's been a guest on this program before, um, uh, yeah, I guess his show is all, all about deep listening, which, yeah, Melbourne Recital Centre is really going to be the perfect venue for that, um, experience in that acoustically treated room.

Can you tell us about the concept for, for that show and what audiences can expect?

Yes, um, I agree that the, the, the venue is going to lend itself really well too.

It's really intimate.

It's a, it's a, like an old school in a way radio show.

Uh, I mean, Derrick Gee, for those who don't know him is really, is an internet personality.

Uh, he has interviewed amazing, uh, artists, uh, international big names, smaller names, uh, but he's just really good at just being able to explain music to, um, to anyone really.

He's, uh, he's really, uh, really embodies, uh, really, uh, what a music critic could be, but in a really conversational way.

Uh, so he has put together, um, his night, um, so he's inviting Julia Jacklin, who's going to be coming, chatting with him, performing, playing some tracks, uh, and, uh, Michael Kucyk, who is, uh, the boss of Efficient Space.

Amazing lineup, um, label as well.

So a really great night of chats and in a living room environment.

Very cool.

And I should say as a bit of a disclaimer, um, through my work at the Wheeler Centre as a programmer, I have been involved in some of, uh, the talks, sort of putting the talks program together with your team at, uh, Now or Never as well.

But there was one I wanted to, I guess, particularly mention that might be of some interest to RRR listeners as it features a lineup of speakers that are sort of very near and dear to many RRR listeners.

Including, um, [name uncertain: Sosefina Fumoli], Sarah Smith as well, um, Al Newstead, who's written a book recently as part of the 33 and a third series on, uh, Tame Impala's currents and hosted by a good friend of this show, Simon Winkler, who of course was the co-host of Breaking and Entering for 18 years.

Um, they're coming together for what should be, yeah, a really fascinating conversation on music criticism that's happening at the Wheeler Centre too.

Great, yes.

Uh, so much to discover as part of Now or Never, um, as well.

Of course, there's some incredible, yeah, large-scale light installations happening along the Birurung Yarra River as well.

Is there anything else in particular you'd like to draw our attention to as part of the program, some of your favourite others?

For you, I think it's, uh, there are different layers, different ways of interacting with, uh, I think, I hope, with, uh, Now or Never.

We have a really large, large program of free, uh, free amazing installations all around the city.

You mentioned the, like, South Bank and we have some projections onto Hammer Hall.

We have an amazing artist, [name uncertain: Aka Cheng] from Taiwan, who's coming for the first time, presenting also a laser installation on the river, uh, reflecting onto the river.

Uh, we have Emily Parsons-Lord, who is an amazing, um, artist based in Melbourne as well, who's going to make the Evan Walker Bridge disappear in mist.

So there will be lots of really large-scale installations all around there.

And then if you start from, um, Melbourne Town Hall and with, uh, Robin Fox, you'll be able to have a full experience of the city being all lit up and, and really seeing amazing artists brought, I think, on a, on a bigger scale.

So, and some really great local talent as well.

Incredible.

Well, congratulations, Elise, on another, yeah, amazing program this year, Now or Never, uh, takes over the city from August 19 to 30.

Uh, and our guest has been the artistic director, Elise Peyronnet from Now or Never.

Thanks so much, Elise.

Thank you, Laura.
